newsitem.title: USA: Arkansas trooper says many Clinton tales "untrue".
newsitem.headline: Arkansas trooper says many Clinton tales "untrue".

text.p: An Arkansas state trooper interviewed in this week's New Yorker magazine said many stories attributed to state troopers about President Bill Clinton's reputed extramarital affairs were not true.

Ronald Anderson, a member of then-Arkansas Gov. Clinton's security detail, said in a 1994 affidavit released to the magazine that, in early discussions about a possible book deal, he had confirmed stories regarding Clinton's alleged infidelity although he knew they were untrue.
He said he knew many of those stories either "to be untrue" or that he had no first-hand knowledge of them.
While he said he could not discredit all the stories, he said many "were nothing more than old fish tales, with little, if any, basis in fact." The affidavit was made by Clinton's lawyers.

Anderson's revelations appear in an article about the case filed against Clinton by Paula Jones, a former Arkansas state employee who is suing the president for alleged sexual harassment. Clinton has denied the allegations.

The state trooper said he confirmed the stories about Clinton because after the 1992 Democratic Convention, he and other troopers believed they could make money by selling their stories to a book publisher.
Anderson also said a longtime political foe of Clinton's, an Arkansas attorney named Cliff Jackson, urged the troopers to release their stories to magazine and newspaper reporters.
In exchange, Anderson said in the magazine that the attorney offered them jobs outside Arkansas for seven years at an annual salary of $100,000.
Anderson told the New Yorker he would not sign a release because of the "lies and inaccuracies" in the other troopers' stories.
Jackson told Reuters that Anderson's allegations were "just ridiculous," but said he had offered to help the troopers get jobs if they got fired. "It was never necessary," he said.
Jackson said he had never helped Jones in her case against Clinton. "I have made it very clear that I think the last thing this country needs is another failed presidency or an impeachment," he said.
In Newsweek magazine on Sunday, aides to Whitewater special prosecutor Kenneth Starr admitted it was "unwise" of FBI agents to ask about Jones while probing Clinton's private life for Starr.
The New Yorker article also cited two friends of Jones who said after her encounter with Clinton, she was "elated." One described her "bubbly enthusiasm" after meeting him.
